title: Obstacle-avoiding robot
desc: Ultrasonic sensor steers the robot around obstacles
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno R3 development board (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB A-to-B cable (for programming the Arduino) (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor (Pixel Electronics – pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x SG90 micro servo motor (used to sweep the ultrasonic sensor left/right) (Pixel Electronics – pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x L298N dual H-bridge motor driver module (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)
  • 2 x DC gear motors with wheels (or 4 motors for a 4WD chassis) (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Robot chassis kit (acrylic or plastic base plate with caster/support wheel) (Pixel Electronics – pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x 4xAA battery holder with on/off switch, or 1 x 7.4V Li-ion battery pack with holder (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Small breadboard (for tidy sensor wiring) (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)
  • 20 x Male-to-male jumper wires (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)
  • 10 x Male-to-female jumper wires (Pixel Electronics – pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Small screwdriver set (for chassis assembly) (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)
  • Cable ties or double-sided foam tape (for mounting the sensor/servo/battery) (Nerokas – nerokas.co.ke)

How It Works

This robot uses an ultrasonic sensor to "see" without eyes. The sensor sends out a sound wave that is too high-pitched for humans to hear, then listens for the echo bouncing back off any object in front of it. Because sound travels at a known, steady speed, the Arduino can measure how long the echo takes to return and calculate exactly how far away the object is — the same trick bats and dolphins use to navigate in the dark.

A small servo motor holds the ultrasonic sensor and swings it left and right, like a head turning to look around. This lets the robot check for open space on either side whenever it finds something blocking the path ahead.

The robot's wheels are driven by two DC motors connected to a motor driver board (the L298N). DC motors need more current than the Arduino's pins can safely provide, so the driver acts like a set of controlled switches/amplifiers: the Arduino sends small "instruction" signals, and the driver uses the battery's power to actually spin the wheels forward, backward, or stop them.

Putting it together: the Arduino constantly asks the ultrasonic sensor "how far is the nearest thing in front of me?" If the answer is a large number (clear path), it drives forward. If the number drops below a set distance (an obstacle is close), the robot stops, turns its "head" left and right to compare distances, and then steers toward whichever side has more open space — just like a person peeking around a corner before deciding which way to walk.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Assemble the robot chassis first: attach the two DC motors and wheels to the base plate, and fix the caster/support wheel at the front or back for balance. Do not attach the electronics yet.
  2. Mount the L298N motor driver on top of the chassis using screws or double-sided tape, positioned so its wires can easily reach both motors and the Arduino.
  3. Wire the motors to the L298N: connect the left motor's two wires to OUT1 and OUT2, and the right motor's two wires to OUT3 and OUT4. Polarity determines direction — this can be corrected in software later, so do not worry about getting it "perfectly right" yet.
  4. Wire the L298N to the Arduino: IN1→pin 8, IN2→pin 9, IN3→pin 10, IN4→pin 11, ENA→pin 5 (PWM), ENB→pin 6 (PWM). Connect the L298N's GND to the Arduino's GND — this shared ground is essential for the signals to work.
  5. Connect the battery pack's positive and negative wires to the L298N's power input terminals (12V/VCC and GND), not directly to the Arduino. Leave the switch off for now.
  6. Mount the SG90 servo at the front of the chassis (facing forward) and attach the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor to the servo's horn/arm using tape or a small bracket, so the sensor can rotate with the servo.
  7. Wire the servo: red wire to Arduino 5V, brown/black wire to Arduino GND, orange/signal wire to Arduino pin 3.
  8. Wire the ultrasonic sensor: VCC to 5V, GND to GND, TRIG to pin 12, ECHO to pin 13.
  9. Double-check that ALL grounds (Arduino, L298N, servo, sensor) are connected together — this is the most common source of strange behaviour if missed.
  10. Connect the Arduino to the laptop via USB, open the Arduino IDE, and upload the sketch below. Students should watch the servo sweep and confirm the Serial Monitor shows changing distance readings as they wave a hand in front of the sensor.
  11. Disconnect USB, place the robot on the floor with open space around it, switch on the battery pack, and observe. The robot should drive forward, then stop, look left and right, and turn away from any obstacle placed in its path.
  12. If the robot turns the wrong way, spins in place instead of driving straight, or drives backward when it should go forward, swap the relevant motor wires on the L298N and re-test.
  13. Once basic obstacle avoidance works, let students test with different obstacles (books, chair legs, walls) and adjust the stopping distance in the code together as a class.

Full Code


#include <Servo.h>             // Library that lets us control the servo motor easily

// ---------- Pin definitions ----------
const int trigPin = 12;        // Sends the ultrasonic "ping"
const int echoPin = 13;        // Receives the echo back
const int servoPin = 3;        // Controls the servo that sweeps the sensor

const int IN1 = 8;             // Left motor direction pin A
const int IN2 = 9;             // Left motor direction pin B
const int IN3 = 10;            // Right motor direction pin A
const int IN4 = 11;            // Right motor direction pin B
const int ENA = 5;             // Left motor speed (PWM)
const int ENB = 6;             // Right motor speed (PWM)

Servo scanServo;                // Create a servo object to control the sweeping head

const int STOP_DISTANCE = 20;   // If something is closer than this (cm), stop and turn
const int MOTOR_SPEED = 150;    // Speed value from 0 (stopped) to 255 (full speed)

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);           // Start serial communication so we can see distance readings

  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT);     // Trig sends a signal out
  pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);      // Echo listens for the signal coming back

  pinMode(IN1, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(IN2, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(IN3, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(IN4, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ENA, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ENB, OUTPUT);

  scanServo.attach(servoPin);   // Tell the servo library which pin the servo is on
  scanServo.write(90);          // Start with the sensor facing straight ahead
  delay(500);                   // Give the servo time to reach that position
}

void loop() {
  int distanceAhead = getDistance();     // Measure what is directly in front

  Serial.print("Distance ahead: ");      // Print reading so students can watch it live
  Serial.println(distanceAhead);

  if (distanceAhead > STOP_DISTANCE) {
    moveForward();                       // Path is clear, keep driving
  } else {
    stopMotors();                        // Something is close, stop first
    delay(200);

    int distanceLeft = lookDirection(30);   // Turn head left and measure
    delay(200);
    int distanceRight = lookDirection(150); // Turn head right and measure
    delay(200);

    scanServo.write(90);                    // Return head to centre
    delay(300);

    if (distanceLeft > distanceRight) {
      turnLeft();                           // More space on the left, so turn that way
      delay(400);
    } else {
      turnRight();                          // More space on the right (or equal), turn that way
      delay(400);
    }
    stopMotors();                           // Stop briefly before trying forward again
  }
}

// Moves the servo to a given angle, waits for it to settle, and returns the distance reading
int lookDirection(int angle) {
  scanServo.write(angle);        // Rotate the sensor head
  delay(400);                    // Wait for the servo to physically get there
  return getDistance();          // Take a fresh reading at this new angle
}

// Sends an ultrasonic pulse and calculates distance in centimetres from the echo time
int getDistance() {
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);    // Make sure trig starts LOW
  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH);   // Send a short 10-microsecond pulse
  delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);

  long duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH);  // Measures how long (in microseconds) the echo pin stays HIGH
  int distance = duration * 0.034 / 2;     // Speed of sound (0.034 cm/us), divided by 2 for the round trip

  if (distance == 0) {
    distance = 400;              // If no echo received, assume path is clear (avoids false stops)
  }
  return distance;
}

// ---------- Motor control functions ----------
void moveForward() {
  digitalWrite(IN1, HIGH);       // Left motor spins forward
  digitalWrite(IN2, LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN3, HIGH);       // Right motor spins forward
  digitalWrite(IN4, LOW);
  analogWrite(ENA, MOTOR_SPEED); // Set left motor speed
  analogWrite(ENB, MOTOR_SPEED); // Set right motor speed
}

void turnLeft() {
  digitalWrite(IN1, LOW);        // Left motor spins backward (or stops)
  digitalWrite(IN2, HIGH);
  digitalWrite(IN3, HIGH);       // Right motor spins forward
  digitalWrite(IN4, LOW);
  analogWrite(ENA, MOTOR_SPEED);
  analogWrite(ENB, MOTOR_SPEED);
}

void turnRight() {
  digitalWrite(IN1, HIGH);       // Left motor spins forward
  digitalWrite(IN2, LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN3, LOW);        // Right motor spins backward (or stops)
  digitalWrite(IN4, HIGH);
  analogWrite(ENA, MOTOR_SPEED);
  analogWrite(ENB, MOTOR_SPEED);
}

void stopMotors() {
  digitalWrite(IN1, LOW);        // All direction pins LOW stops both motors
  digitalWrite(IN2, LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN3, LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN4, LOW);
  analogWrite(ENA, 0);           // Zero speed as an extra safety measure
  analogWrite(ENB, 0);
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Robot spins in circles instead of driving straightOne motor's wires are reversed compared to the otherSwap the two output wires for that motor on the L298N, or swap the corresponding HIGH/LOW values in code
Serial Monitor shows "0" for distance constantlyTrig and Echo pins wired to the wrong Arduino pins, or swapped with each otherRe-check wiring against pin definitions in the code; confirm TRIG and ECHO are not swapped
Servo twitches or resets randomly, sensor readings are erraticServo and sensor are being powered from the Arduino's 5V pin while motors draw heavy current from the same source, causing voltage dipsPower the servo/sensor from Arduino 5V but ensure a strong shared ground with the L298N; if problems persist, power servo from a separate 5V regulator
Robot does not move at all when battery is switched onBattery connected to Arduino instead of L298N power input, or L298N's onboard 5V jumper removed incorrectlyConfirm battery goes to the L298N's power terminals; check the 5V enable jumper is in place if using it to power the Arduino too
Robot drives into obstacles instead of stoppingSTOP_DISTANCE value too small, or ultrasonic sensor aimed too high/low to detect the obstacleIncrease STOP_DISTANCE in code and adjust the sensor's mounting angle so it points level with likely obstacle height
Robot works when plugged into USB power but fails when running on batteryBattery pack is weak, low on charge, or cannot supply enough current for both motors and electronicsUse fresh/charged batteries and confirm the pack's voltage/current rating matches the motors' requirements

Discussion Questions

  • How does the ultrasonic sensor figure out distance without touching the object?
  • Why does the robot need a motor driver instead of connecting the motors straight to the Arduino?
  • What might happen if the servo sweeps too quickly for the ultrasonic sensor to take an accurate reading — how could you test this?
  • Can you think of a real animal or real-world device that uses a similar "send a signal and listen for the echo" idea to sense its surroundings?
  • If you wanted the robot to avoid obstacles even faster, what part of the code or hardware would you change first, and why?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add an LED that lights up whenever the robot detects an obstacle and stops, so people nearby know it is "thinking."
  • Medium: Modify the code so the robot compares three directions (left, centre, right) before deciding where to turn, instead of just left vs right.
